strengths: Addresses a meaningful speech-language-model bottleneck with a coherent codec supporting inference-time rate adjustment and content-dependent allocation below 12.5 Hz.

Strong low-rate intelligibility results: at 6.25 Hz, RVQ-1 reconstruction achieves 4.15% WER versus 31.5% for retrained DualCodec. Comparisons include baselines retrained with the same training recipe and enlarged codebooks.

Controlled ablations provide concrete evidence for dynamic allocation: at 6.25 Hz, it improves RVQ-1 WER from 5.22% to 4.15% and ASR-probing WER from 18.8% to 15.6%. Additional ablations distinguish the roles of semantic features, quantization, and Transformer refinement.

Downstream TTS demonstrates practical utility: reducing the AR rate from 12.5 to approximately 6.25 Hz lowers total RTF from 0.26 to 0.18 with competitive intelligibility and speaker similarity. Architecture and training details are substantial.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily the integration of existing techniques at lower rates. Much of the headline semantic improvement comes from the pretrained ASR encoder: simply replacing DualCodec's SSL features reportedly reaches 6.0% WER. Direct comparisons against existing dynamic-merging approaches using the same encoder would better establish the proposed mechanism's advantage.

The dynamic-rate ablation also changes convolutional strides and intermediate temporal resolution. A fixed or content-independent merging baseline operating on the same 12.5 Hz features would isolate adaptive boundary selection more convincingly. Equal-frame-rate comparisons also give dynamic tokens additional duration bits.

Core reconstruction evaluation is restricted to 1,088 short LibriSpeech test-clean utterances, and rate thresholds were calibrated on that test set. Generalization to noisy speech, conversational speech, and long utterances remains untested; uncertainty estimates are absent for the objective improvements.

Efficiency comparisons need fuller accounting. Table 5 lists 216M parameters, while Appendix F gives 450M including the required frozen ASR encoder. Codec encoding/decoding runtime and memory are not reported, and cross-system TTS speedups are confounded by architecture and implementation differences. The system also lacks streaming support.

Several claims exceed the evidence: 3 Hz operation produces 51.5% RVQ-1 WER, rate control specifies corpus averages rather than guaranteed per-utterance rates, and acoustic superiority is not uniform across metrics. Subjective TTS evaluation uses only ten utterances per system, while the strongest TTS results rely on a separate 50 Hz mel decoder rather than the low-rate codec's acoustic reconstruction path.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful bottleneck in speech language models: preserving intelligibility while reducing autoregressive sequence length. Combining ASR-guided dynamic merging with inference-time rate control provides a useful contribution at frame rates below 12.5 Hz.

The controlled experiments provide concrete support for dynamic allocation. At 6.25 Hz, dynamic merging reduces RVQ-1 reconstruction WER from 5.22% to 4.15% and ASR-probing WER from 18.8% to 15.6% compared with the fixed-rate variant (Table 3). Improvements across both evaluations strengthen the evidence.

Evaluation includes retrained low-rate baselines, numerous public codecs, component ablations, nine understanding tasks, and downstream TTS. The ablations help distinguish the semantic benefits of ASR features from the acoustic benefits of Transformer refinement.

The TTS results demonstrate practical utility: reducing the same system's AR rate from 12.5 to approximately 6.25 Hz lowers total RTF from 0.26 to 0.18, with comparable speaker similarity and a moderate WER increase. Training and architectural details are reasonably extensive.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is primarily an integration of existing techniques. Much of the headline improvement over DualCodec comes from the pretrained ASR representation: simply replacing its SSL features reportedly reduces 6.25 Hz WER from 31.5% to 6.0%, already approaching FlexiCodec's 4.15%. The contribution should be positioned around the additional dynamic-allocation benefit.

The dynamic-rate comparison could isolate the mechanism better. Fixed-rate ablations change encoder and decoder strides, whereas FlexiCodec retains a 12.5 Hz underlying representation. Uniform or random merging on the same representation, with comparable duration overhead, would better establish the value of semantic boundary selection. Related dynamic tokenization methods are discussed but not experimentally compared.

Codec reconstruction evaluation is restricted to 1,088 short LibriSpeech test-clean utterances, and merging thresholds are calibrated on that test set. Held-out calibration and testing on noisy, accented, conversational, and longer speech would substantially strengthen generalization claims. Uncertainty estimates are absent for the principal objective results.

The advertised 3–12.5 Hz operating range needs qualification. At 3 Hz, RVQ-1 WER reaches 51.5%, and even eight quantizers yield 18.1% WER (Table 2). Threshold adjustment controls a content-dependent average rate rather than guaranteeing a requested rate on unseen inputs.

Efficiency and perceptual-quality claims exceed some of the evidence. Table 5 lists 216M trainable parameters although the complete codec includes a 234M frozen ASR encoder; codec encoding latency and memory are not reported. Cross-system TTS speedups are confounded by different architectures, and subjective evaluation uses only ten utterances per system. The strongest TTS quality also requires a 50 Hz acoustic generator, while the 12.5 Hz alternative noticeably degrades quality.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem for speech language models: preserving intelligibility while reducing autoregressive sequence length. Combining ASR-guided frame merging with a reconstructive codec at 6.25–12.5 Hz is a useful contribution.
Semantic preservation is strong. At 6.25 Hz, FlexiCodec achieves 4.15% RVQ-1 reconstruction WER versus 31.5% for retrained DualCodec, alongside competitive acoustic reconstruction metrics.

Controlled ablations provide evidence for dynamic allocation beyond the stronger semantic encoder. At 6.25 Hz, dynamic merging improves RVQ-1 WER from 5.22% to 4.15% and ASR probing WER from 18.8% to 15.6% relative to the fixed-rate variant.

The downstream TTS evaluation demonstrates practical value. With a 50 Hz acoustic decoder, reducing the AR rate from 12.5 to 6.25 Hz lowers total RTF from 0.26 to 0.18 while retaining competitive intelligibility and speaker similarity.

The evaluation includes reconstruction, ASR probing, audio understanding, component ablations, and downstream synthesis. Training configurations and architectural details are substantially documented.
weaknesses: The novelty is primarily an integration and extension of existing techniques. Much of the headline improvement comes from the pretrained ASR representation: simply replacing DualCodec’s SSL features with ASR features reportedly reduces its 6.25 Hz WER to 6.0%. Comparisons with alternative dynamic merging strategies would better establish the distinctive contribution.

The main reconstruction evaluation is restricted to 1,088 short, clean English audiobook utterances. Moreover, the merging thresholds are explicitly selected using trial runs on the test set. Independent validation-set calibration and evaluation on noisy, conversational, and longer speech are needed to establish generalization.

The dynamic-versus-fixed ablation matches frame rate rather than total transmitted information: dynamic tokens additionally carry duration attributes. An equal-bitrate comparison would strengthen claims about compression efficiency.

Efficiency comparisons need more careful qualification. Table 5 reports 216M parameters for FlexiCodec while its complete inference model includes the frozen ASR encoder and totals 450M parameters. Codec encoding/decoding runtime and memory are not reported, and cross-system TTS speedups are confounded by architectural differences. The current codec also does not support streaming.

Perceptual evidence is limited. Codec reconstruction quality relies on objective metrics, while the TTS listening study uses only 10 utterances per system and six raters. No confidence intervals or significance tests establish whether the small perceptual gains are reliable.

Several claims exceed the evidence. At 3 Hz, RVQ-1 WER reaches 51.5%, so controllability should be distinguished from useful low-rate performance. Acoustic superiority is not uniform across metrics, and the claim that a higher NAR frame rate is essential is confounded by changing the predicted representation and decoder.

strengths: FlexiCodec addresses a meaningful problem for speech language models: preserving intelligibility while reducing autoregressive sequence length. Its ASR-guided dynamic merging supports multiple inference-time frame rates within one model and explicitly accounts for duration metadata in reported bitrates.

The low-frame-rate results are strong. At 6.25Hz, semantic-only reconstruction achieves 4.15% WER, compared with 31.5% for retrained DualCodec. More importantly, the controlled fixed-rate FlexiCodec comparison supports an additional benefit from dynamic allocation: WER improves from 5.22% to 4.15%, and ASR probing WER improves from 18.8% to 15.6%.

The evaluation is substantial, covering retrained baselines, numerous public codecs, component ablations, ASR probing, audio understanding, out-of-domain English, multilingual transfer, and runtime. The factorial analysis usefully acknowledges that ASR features account for most of the headline semantic improvement.

The downstream TTS results provide concrete practical evidence. With a 50Hz acoustic decoder, the 6.25Hz setting matches CosyVoice's reported 3.2% WER while reducing measured total RTF from 0.62 to 0.18. Within-model frame-rate comparisons also demonstrate a useful efficiency-quality trade-off.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental: dual-stream semantic/acoustic coding, ASR features, token merging, Transformer bottlenecks, and FSQ build on existing ideas. Table 9 shows that replacing SSL features with SenseVoice alone reduces WER from 31.5% to 5.99%. Comparisons against cited dynamic-rate approaches such as CodecSlime, TFC, and VARSTok are missing, leaving the advantage of this particular merging strategy insufficiently established.

The dynamic-rate ablation does not completely isolate adaptive allocation. Fixed-rate variants change convolutional strides, whereas the proposed system retains a 12.5Hz representation before merging. A uniform-merging control using the same architecture would be cleaner. Furthermore, dynamic semantic tokens include three duration bits beyond the 15-bit token index; equal-frame-rate comparisons therefore do not establish equal-bitrate superiority.

Evaluation uncertainty is insufficiently characterized. Objective results lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variability, despite several small differences. TTS subjective evaluation uses only 10 utterances per system and six raters, with large reported spreads. Frame-rate thresholds are calibrated on the test sets rather than a separate validation set, weakening the independence of the evaluation protocol.

Some claims exceed the demonstrated operating range. At 3Hz, semantic-only WER reaches 51.5% and eight-layer WER reaches 18.1%, so controllability down to 3Hz should not imply useful high-quality operation throughout that range. Acoustic superiority is also metric-dependent: competing codecs outperform FlexiCodec on some PESQ, UTMOS, and speaker-similarity comparisons.

The strongest TTS results use a separate 50Hz mel-spectrogram decoder; the 12.5Hz codec-feature decoder substantially degrades quality. These results support compact semantic conditioning more strongly than an end-to-end low-frame-rate synthesis pipeline. Cross-system speedups also involve different architectures, and full-utterance GPU RTF does not establish streaming latency or suitability for resource-constrained devices.

Generalization remains limited for the semantic stream: zero-shot non-English RVQ-1 WER is often extremely high. Reporting also needs reconciliation: Appendix J incorrectly states that multilingual evaluation has not been conducted, despite Appendix F, and Table 5's 216M parameter count excludes the frozen encoder required for encoding, while Appendix H reports 450M total parameters.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing speech-token sequence lengths while preserving intelligibility. A single codec supports variable inference-time frame rates with explicit duration information and reconstructible audio.

The controlled comparisons provide concrete evidence for dynamic allocation. At 6.25Hz, it reduces RVQ-1 reconstruction WER from 5.22% to 4.15% and ASR-probing WER from 18.8% to 15.6% relative to the fixed-rate variant (Table 3). These improvements go beyond simply adopting ASR features.

The evaluation is substantial: retrained low-rate baselines, numerous public codecs, component ablations, downstream TTS and understanding tasks, encoding/decoding benchmarks, and out-of-domain and multilingual tests. Appendix D usefully identifies the contribution of individual design choices.

The TTS experiments demonstrate practical benefits. Within the same 50Hz acoustic-decoder configuration, reducing the AR rate from 12.5Hz to approximately 6.25Hz lowers total RTF from 0.26 to 0.18 while maintaining speaker similarity, although WER increases from 2.5% to 3.2%.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental. The architecture combines established dual-stream coding, pretrained ASR features, similarity-based merging, Transformer refinement, and FSQ. Table 9 shows that most of the headline improvement over DualCodec comes from replacing SSL features with SenseVoice features: WER falls from 31.5% to 5.99% before introducing the other components.

The dynamic-merging evaluation does not fully isolate the proposed segmentation rule. Fixed-rate ablations also change encoder strides, and there are no matched comparisons against uniform merging on the same 12.5Hz features, random boundaries, or alternative semantic segmentation methods. Such controls would strengthen attribution to phonetic adaptivity.

Evaluation uncertainty is insufficiently characterized. No repeated-run variation or confidence intervals accompany the central codec improvements, and the TTS listening study uses only ten utterances per system. Merging thresholds are calibrated using the test set, including per-language calibration, rather than a separate development set.

Several claims exceed the demonstrated operating range. At 3Hz, RVQ-1 WER is 51.5% and eight-layer WER is 18.1%, so controllability does not establish useful high-quality operation throughout 3–12.5Hz. Acoustic superiority is also metric-dependent: competing methods outperform FlexiCodec on some speaker-similarity, PESQ, and UTMOS comparisons.

Efficiency and generality require qualification. The full codec includes approximately 450M parameters, although the main comparison lists 216M trainable parameters; it operates on complete utterances and does not support streaming. Cross-system TTS speedups do not isolate token-rate effects from architectural differences, and multilingual RVQ-1 intelligibility often collapses without adaptation. These limitations weaken claims about low-latency deployment and broadly applicable semantic representations.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: reducing speech-token sequence lengths while retaining intelligibility. A single codec supports inference-time rate adjustment and reconstructible speech below 10 Hz.
Strong low-rate results: at 6.25 Hz, FlexiCodec achieves 4.15% WER from semantic tokens and 2.53% with eight quantizers, substantially outperforming the retrained DAC and DualCodec baselines.

Controlled ablations substantiate dynamic merging beyond the ASR feature choice: at 6.25 Hz, it improves semantic-token WER from 5.22% to 4.15% and ASR-probing WER from 18.8% to 15.6%. Additional ablations clarify the contributions of transformers and quantization.

Evaluation is relatively extensive, covering numerous codecs, downstream TTS, audio understanding, out-of-domain English, multilingual transfer, and runtime. TTS demonstrates a useful within-model speed–quality tradeoff, reducing total RTF from 0.26 to 0.18 when lowering the AR rate.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental, combining existing dual-stream codecs, pretrained ASR features, similarity-based merging, and transformer refinement. Table 9 shows that replacing SSL features with SenseVoice accounts for most of the headline WER improvement, from 31.5% to 5.99%. Comparisons against alternative merging strategies would better establish the distinctive contribution.

Fixed-rate ablations match frame rate but do not fully match information budget: dynamic tokens additionally transmit three duration bits per frame, a 20% overhead relative to the 15-bit semantic token. Matched-total-bitrate comparisons would strengthen the semantic compression claim.

Evaluation uncertainty is insufficiently characterized. Objective improvements lack confidence intervals or repeated runs, codec reconstruction has no direct listening study, and TTS subjective evaluation uses only ten utterances per system and six listeners. Small perceptual differences therefore remain inconclusive.

Frame-rate thresholds are calibrated on the evaluation sets, including separately for each tested language. Held-out calibration and reporting achieved rates under distribution shift are needed to substantiate practical rate controllability. At 3 Hz, semantic-token WER reaches 51.5%, substantially limiting the useful operating range.

Cross-system TTS speedups conflate tokenizer rate with architecture, training, and implementation differences. The strongest quality results use a 50 Hz mel decoder; the 12.5 Hz codec-feature decoder substantially reduces speaker similarity and subjective quality. Full-utterance operation also limits low-latency deployment claims.

Generalization and reporting have limitations: zero-shot semantic-token WER approaches 100% for several languages, the limitations section contradicts the multilingual experiments, and the supplied manuscript has blank code and demo links. Architecture and training details are substantial, but implementation availability cannot be verified.
